passages.text: Simon said, “You have said these things correctly. Yet in the present world, does it not seem to you that a human being is susceptible to every passion? I mean desire, anger, grief, and such things.” Peter said, “These too belong to the things that happen, not to the things that always exist. They will now be found to occur usefully for the soul. For desire has been made to occur in the living being by the one who made everything well, so that, led by it into intercourse, it may multiply humanity. From humanity a multitude of chosen better people arises, suitable for eternal life. But without desire no one would have undertaken intercourse with a woman; as it is, under the pretext of pleasure, as though gratifying himself, the human being does that one’s will. Yet if someone uses desire for lawful marriage, he does not act impiously. If he rushes toward adultery, he acts impiously and for this reason is punished, because he used badly what was established well. Likewise, anger has received from God the nature of being kindled within us, so that we may be drawn by it to resist sins. Yet someone who uses it without measure does wrong, while one who uses it as deserved accomplishes what is just. We are also susceptible to grief, so that we may have sympathy at the death of those close to us—a wife, children, brothers, parents, friends, or others. For if we did not have the capacity to share suffering, we would be inhuman. All the other things likewise will be found to be fitting, if the reason why they came into being is understood.”

lexical_decisions.rationale: Occurrences are contrasted with things existing always; “accidents” in a technical philosophical sense is possible but misleading without explanation.

The immediate purpose of multiplying humanity supports the sexual sense of participation or sharing here. The text adds no sexual detail or named partners beyond the ensuing woman and lawful marriage.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a multitude of chosen better people
lexical_decisions.rationale: The compact genitives can alternatively mean “a multitude from which better people are selected.” The main text takes ἐκλογῆς as characterizing the resultant multitude by selection, retaining κρειττόνων as the selected better people; it does not uniquely settle how the selection is made.
ἄμυνα can mean defense against or requital of offenses. The main text takes the first, while “to punish offenses” is a material alternative in view of the ensuing measured use of anger.
The term can indicate proportional worth or due measure; the main text does not make every expression of anger just.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οἰκείων, γυναικὸς ἢ τέκνων ἢ ἀδελ-. φῶν ἢ γονέων ἢ φίλων ἢ ἄλλων τινῶν
lexical_decisions.chosen: those close to us—a wife, children, brothers, parents, friends, or others
lexical_decisions.rationale: οἰκεῖοι can mean household members, relatives, or people close to someone. Friends and other people in the ensuing list support the broader relational sense, avoiding an added household-membership restriction. The printed word division ἀδελ-. φῶν is represented as the intact word “brothers”; the single dot with a hyphen is not treated as a multi-dot lacuna or recovered missing word.

passages.text: Simon said, “Why, then, do people also die before their time, and why do recurring illnesses arise? Moreover, why are there demons, madness, and sufferings of every kind, capable of inflicting great punishment?” Peter said, “Because people devote everything of their own to pleasure, have intercourse without observing the proper times, and thus the depositing of seed, offered at the wrong time, naturally grows countless evils. They should have reasoned that, just as a suitable time for planting and sowing has been appointed, so days requiring observance have been assigned for intercourse. Hence someone who had learned from the tradition of Moses, reproaching the people for sins, called them sons of lunar new moons and sabbaths. At the beginning of the world people were also long-lived and free of illness. But when, through neglect, they abandoned the observance, from that time sons in succession, because of ignorance, ..... having intercourse when they should not, place their own children under countless sufferings. Hence also our [..... αλος], concerning the person disabled from birth who received sight from him, [ἔξετα .............. εν] this man or his parents, he was born blind, answered, ‘Neither did this man sin in any way, nor his parents, but so that through him the power of God might be revealed,’ healing the sins of ignorance. And indeed such things happen because of ignorance: that is, not knowing when one should have intercourse with one’s wife, whether she is clean from menstruation. Yet the sufferings you mentioned come from ignorance; they are not, however, brought about by the evil one. Moreover, give me someone who does not sin, and receive someone who does not suffer; and besides not suffering, you will find him able to heal others as well. Moses, for example, through reverence for God continued without suffering throughout his whole life, and by prayers healed the Egyptians who suffered because of sins.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: have intercourse without observing the proper times
lexical_decisions.rationale: The following planting analogy and days to observe specify the context of observance; “without precaution” is less specific. This is the ancient speaker’s explanation, not independent medical advice.
The adjective denotes periodic or cyclical occurrence, not a specific diagnosis.
The historical categories are retained, not collapsed into a modern psychiatric equivalence.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: υἱοὺς νεομηνιῶν τῶν κατὰ σελήνην καὶ σαββάτων
lexical_decisions.chosen: sons of lunar new moons and sabbaths
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source explicitly connects the days with the sons in its argument. No prophet’s name or external quotation is supplied.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: οὔτε οὗτός τι ἥμαρτεν οὔτε οἱ γονεῖς αὐτοῦ
lexical_decisions.chosen: Neither did this man sin in any way, nor his parents
lexical_decisions.rationale: This rendering follows the wording of this author’s quotation, without importing differently worded biblical translations.

lexical_decisions.chosen: whether she is clean from menstruation
lexical_decisions.rationale: The purity category is the speaker’s, not an added biological assertion. “Whether she has become clean after menstruation” is another contextual rendering.
The feminine participle can agree with δύναμις, power, in the quotation; its action is not assigned to a uniquely named person by the English.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ πρὸς τὸ μὴ πάσχειν καὶ ἄλλους αὐτὸν θεραπεῦσαι δυνάμενος εὕρῃς.
lexical_decisions.chosen: and besides not suffering, you will find him able to heal others as well
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied δυνάμενος is nominative, not accusative δυνάμενον. The main English understands the healing ability as predicated of αὐτόν, the sinless person found, despite that case mismatch; the immediately following example of Moses’ freedom from suffering and healing others supports this contextual construal. A material alternative attaches the nominative participle to the addressed person: “and besides not suffering, you, being able to heal others as well, may find him.” That changes the possessor of healing ability. The supplied spelling and case are retained, not silently normalized or characterized as an OCR error. The English choice is not claimed as the uniquely regular grammatical reading.

source_issues.source_quote: υἱοὶ ἀγνοίας αἰτίᾳ ..... μὴ δεῖν κοινωνοῦντες
source_issues.issue: The five-dot printed gap is retained exactly. The sentence stays visibly incomplete at the link between the sons, ignorance, and intercourse that should not take place; no missing connective or argument is restored.
The five-dot gap and surviving αλος are retained literally as [..... αλος]. The partial word is not completed to a title or person’s name.

source_issues.source_quote: ἔξετα .............. εν οὗτος ἢ οἱ γονεῖς αὐτοῦ τυφλὸς ἐγεννήθη
source_issues.issue: The surviving ἔξετα and εν flank a fourteen-dot printed gap, all retained literally as [ἔξετα .............. εν]. The subsequent surviving “this man or his parents” and “he was born blind” are represented as incomplete syntax, not joined by a restored question about sin from an external biblical text. No lost words are recovered.

passages.text: When Simon heard these things, he said, “Do not suppose that, because in examining each topic I agreed, I was proceeding to another topic because I was fully convinced. I was providing you [ἀλ.....νοίας] of being persuaded, so that you would move to another topic, in order that, having learned all your [......... νοίας], I might condemn you without guessing. But [πεπληροφορημε ............]. Now allow me three days, and I will come and show that you know nothing.” After Simon said this and was about to leave, my father said, “Simon, hear a few words from me, and then go as you please. I remember that at the beginning, before the inquiry, having not yet tested me, you leveled preconceived judgments against me. But now, after hearing the discussion continuously, recognizing Peter’s superiority, and now granting him truthfulness, what do I seem to you? Someone who knows how to judge rightly, or not? For if you say that I judged rightly but do not agree, you appear prejudiced, unwilling even after acknowledgment to agree to defeat. But if I did not rightly declare Peter superior in the inquiry, persuade us how we judged incorrectly—or do not stop debating with him before everyone. For, each time being defeated and agreeing, and, if you have a sense of shame, being condemned by all the hearers in place of a most severe punishment and behaving disgracefully, you will suffer pain in your own soul through conscience. For we have seen your defeat in action, but have heard your words of promise. In the end, then, I do not think you will come to the inquiry as you promised; rather, to appear unashamed, you have promised as you leave to return.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: you leveled preconceived judgments against me
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive refers to judgments concerning the father, not necessarily the father’s own prejudices. “You cast down my preconceptions” is a grammatical alternative, but the following reminder of Simon’s failure to test the speaker favors accusations about him.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in place of a most severe punishment
lexical_decisions.rationale: The preposition can convey a replacement or an equivalent penalty. The condemnation is not made a separate physical punishment.

lexical_decisions.chosen: but have heard your words of promise
lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle ἐπαγγελλόμενον is understood as promise-making or professing, describing the speech that has actually been heard. δέ contrasts those words of promise with the defeat already seen in action; the following prediction that Simon will not return reinforces that distinction. A possible alternative treats λόγον as the substantive argument Simon promises to present, “your promised argument,” but the main text avoids suggesting that this future argument has already been delivered. The singular λόγος is expressed collectively as “words,” not as several distinct unprinted promises.
This can indicate not being ashamed or not losing face. It does not assert that Simon lacks every moral sense of shame.

source_issues.issue: The incomplete ἀλ.....νοίας, with exactly five dots, is retained literally. The main text translates the surviving giving and being-persuaded wording but does not complete this word as “signs,” “pretenses,” or any other conjecture.
The nine-dot gap and surviving νοίας are retained literally. The feminine plural “all” and possessive “your” are translated, without recovering the missing word.

The surviving partial participial stem and twelve-dot gap are retained literally after “But.” The stem relates to full assurance, but its lost completion and syntactic continuation are not restored, and no claim that Simon is now convinced is invented.

passages.text: When Simon heard this, he ground his teeth in anger and went away silently. Since a considerable part of the day still remained, Peter laid hands on the large crowd for healing and dismissed them, then went indoors with his closest companions and sat down. One of the followers, named Sophonias, said, “Blessed, Peter, is the God who chose you and filled you with wisdom for the sake of those of good judgment. For you truly discussed with Simon impressively and without resentment. We ask you also to discuss evil things with us, hoping you will disclose the account concerning him more candidly to us—and not at this very hour, but tomorrow, if you please. For we make allowance for your weariness from the inquiry.” Peter said, “I want you to know that someone who does something with pleasure is refreshed by the very exertions, whereas someone who does not do what he wishes is greatly wearied by the rest itself. So you grant me great rest by making me discuss what I enjoy.” Yet, content with his willingness and making allowance for his exertions, we asked that the postponement be until night, as was his custom, for speech to be directed to the [γνησι.....]. And, having partaken of salt, to sleep [........πημεν].

lexical_decisions.rationale: The selected text has a plural, while the following περὶ αὐτοῦ is singular. “About evil people” or “evil ones” is an alternative for the plural; the main text retains that plural-to-singular shift rather than silently regularizing both to “the evil one.”
The comparative can mean more genuinely, sincerely, or intimately. The context requests a fuller disclosure to close associates, not a claim that Peter’s prior argument was false.
The adverb conveys patient endurance of ill-treatment. “Forbearingly” is a concise alternative, less accessible in modern English.

The main text relates the temporal phrase to the requested postponement. Another attachment lets it describe making allowance for his exertions into the night; the surrounding account of his custom supports night as the deferred discussion time.

source_issues.issue: The five-dot gap after γνησι is preserved literally. The surviving πρὸς τοὺς is translated as “to the” and the surviving λέγεσθαι is taken passively as speech being directed or spoken. The stem γνησι points toward genuineness or close association, but its completion is not supplied. Missing wording could affect the infinitive’s construction or even contain a lost compound prefix, so “to converse with the ...” is a contextual alternative, not a recovered reading. The main text nominalizes the surviving speaking verb as “speech” to give readable English without inventing the content of speech. No lost words have been recovered.

The eight-dot gap and surviving ending πημεν are retained as [........πημεν] after “to sleep.” A conventional narrative formula could suggest a verb such as “turned,” but it is not restored from analogy or another passage.

The selected, image-checked source prints συγγόντες. The usual aorist participle of συγγιγνώσκω would be συγγνόντες, but that is only a proposed normalization, not the supplied form. “Making allowance for his exertions” is a contextual construal supported by the earlier συγγινώσκομεν γάρ σοι διὰ τοὺς ἐκ τῆς ζητήσεως καμάτους, “we make allowance for your weariness from the inquiry.” The unusual spelling remains in the selected source and is disclosed rather than silently replaced or labelled an OCR error. No missing print-verification evidence is alleged.
